title: Three companion apps behind my autobattler (in Rust)
author: wdroz
selftext:
Beastforger, my fantasy idle autobattler, released last week. You forge monsters, build teams, and fuse Heroic units. Here's the stack and the companion tools I used to develop it.

The game uses **Rust + Macroquad**. The three local companions use **Tauri 2**, Rust backends, and plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript. Rust's type system and compiler diagnostics give Codex concrete feedback when an edit breaks an interface. The same deterministic rules also run headlessly in tests and balance benchmarks.

The main downside for me is **development disk usage**. The game and companions are separate Cargo projects with their own `target/` directories. Dependency artifacts, debug symbols, and incremental caches accumulate across builds, so even small tools can leave large build folders.

The companions handle three recurring tasks:

* **Fusion Workshop:** choose two Heroic parents from the game catalog; Codex proposes three illustrated concepts. Selecting one saves a Markdown/JSON design contract, portrait, and parent references. A later implementation session adds the playable mechanics, sprites, and tests.
* **Animation Workshop:** inspect the runtime manifests, pause an animation, and step to the exact problem frame. A repair report preserves the prompt, frame metadata, atlas, and manifest snapshot for the next session.
* **Sound Workshop:** select a real attack or game event, compare three ElevenLabs sound-effect candidates, and install the selected cue with its prompt and generation metadata.

For art, **sprite-gen** takes a locked character identity through generated pose rows, background cleanup, frame extraction, alignment, and atlas composition. Higher ranks derive from the previous identity, and attack releases follow the actual combat events.

Codex helps with implementation and reusable task instructions. I still choose the direction, inspect assets, playtest, and decide what stays. Tests and benchmarks check rules and balance; visual review catches drifting proportions, unreadable silhouettes, and awkward animation that a successful build cannot judge.

For me, one of the most underrated strengths of AI-assisted gamedev is how quickly you can build small companion apps tailored to your own workflow.
